betaine.text: Users take betaine as a training supplement, hoping for more strength and power and a fuller, better-hydrated muscle look. Small trials have measured strength and body composition, with mixed results. Claims about cortisol and overtraining rest mostly on limited or anecdotal reports.

ashwagandha.text: Ashwagandha is taken as an adaptogen to lower stress, improve sleep and nudge testosterone, so that users recover and train harder in pursuit of a more muscular physique. Small human trials report modest changes in strength, stress scores and some hormone readings; visible appearance changes have not been directly studied.

turkesterone.text: Turkesterone is promoted to bodybuilders as a natural alternative to anabolic steroids, with users hoping for muscle growth without suppressing their own hormones. Human evidence for muscle gain is largely absent; supporting claims come mainly from animal and cell studies, sellers' marketing and anecdote.

ecdysterone.text: Ecdysterone is taken by lifters as a plant-derived anabolic, with some users promoting it as a hormone-neutral way to add muscle. One small human trial reported greater muscle gain with training, and cell and animal studies point to estrogen receptor beta; evidence is preliminary and product quality is a recurring concern.

chain: Leaner, more masculine physique and face
testosterone.text: Testosterone is discussed in looksmaxxing circles both as the hormone behind masculine features (muscle, jaw and brow development, body hair, voice) and as a therapy (TRT) or high-level drug for physique. Its muscle effects are well studied in medical and trial settings; claims about enhancing facial structure in adults are mostly anecdotal.

somatropin.text: Users take synthetic growth hormone for muscle, fat loss, anti-ageing and, in bodybuilding circles, a so-called steroid look with wider jaw and face. It is approved for deficiency states, and its body-composition effects are studied there; use in healthy adults for appearance is off-label and the facial claims are anecdotal.

chain: Better recovery and sleep, more appetite
mk-677.text: MK-677 is an oral ghrelin mimic that users take to raise growth hormone for recovery, sleep, bulking and, among younger users, possible height. Trials show raised GH and IGF-1 and some lean-mass change in other populations; an aesthetic benefit is unproven and appetite increase is a known effect.

cjc-1295.text: CJC-1295 is an injectable peptide that users take to raise growth hormone for recovery, fat loss, skin and sleep, and some younger users hope for height. Human data are limited to a few endocrine studies showing raised GH and IGF-1; the appearance claims are untested and rest on anecdote.

chain: Possible growth while plates are open
ipamorelin.text: Ipamorelin is a GH-releasing peptide that users, often teenagers or young adults, take hoping for height, better sleep, recovery and facial bone growth, frequently alongside CJC-1295. Human data are thin and focused on GH release; the height and facial claims are untested and largely anecdotal.

sermorelin.text: Sermorelin is a GHRH analogue that users take hoping to raise growth hormone for height in teenagers, leanness, sleep and anti-ageing. It was approved in the past for diagnosing and treating GH deficiency in children; its use for cosmetic or height goals in healthy people is off-label and untested.

ghrp-6.text: GHRP-6 is a GH-releasing peptide that users take to raise growth hormone for muscle, recovery and fat loss, and for the strong hunger it causes, which some use to aid bulking. It has been studied in humans for GH release; the effect on physique is untested and anecdotal.

igf-1-lr3.text: IGF-1 LR3 is an injectable growth-factor analogue sold to bodybuilders for muscle growth and healing, sometimes stacked with insulin or steroids. Reliable human evidence for muscle gain is lacking; claims about local injection growth, bloat and detectability come from forums and vendors.

follistatin-344.text: Follistatin-344 is an unapproved injectable sold to people hoping to block myostatin and build muscle beyond natural limits. The protein has been studied in animals and in gene-therapy research, but injected vendor products are untested for this use in humans; food and training claims are mostly anecdotal.

chain: Lean mass gain, some fat loss
ostarine.text: Ostarine is a SARM used by lifters for lean mass and a leaner look, sometimes alongside TRT or after steroid cycles. It has been trialled for muscle wasting and showed lean-mass gains in those settings; use for aesthetics is off-label, and hormone suppression is a documented effect.

lgd-4033.text: LGD-4033 is a SARM used by lifters to add lean mass in a few weeks with less perceived hormonal impact than steroids. Small trials in older and young men showed lean-mass gains alongside hormonal suppression and lipid changes; evidence for aesthetic use is limited, and product mislabelling is a reported issue.

rad-140.text: RAD-140 is a potent SARM used by lifters for muscle and fat loss, with some hoping for less suppression than steroids. It has been studied in animals and is under development for breast cancer; human evidence for physique use is lacking, with liver and hormone effects reported.

yk-11.text: YK-11 is a steroid-like compound sold as a myostatin-inhibiting SARM, which users take hoping for gains beyond ordinary SARMs. Evidence is limited to cell and animal work; reliable human studies of muscle gain are absent, and its classification is itself disputed.

finasteride.text: Finasteride is an approved oral drug that lowers DHT, used in looksmaxxing circles to stop male pattern hair loss and keep the hairline. It is well studied for this use in men; reported sexual and mood side effects, including persistent ones, are a major point of debate, as are lower and topical regimens.

dutasteride.text: Dutasteride blocks both 5-alpha-reductase types and is used off-label in most countries to stop male pattern hair loss, often as a stronger option than finasteride. It is approved for hair loss in a few countries and has trial data there; reported side effects and topical use are debated.

minoxidil.text: Minoxidil is used to regrow and thicken scalp hair, and many users also apply it to the beard and brows. Topical forms are approved for scalp hair loss; oral low-dose use is off-label with growing trial data, while beard and brow use is less studied.

bimatoprost.text: Bimatoprost is approved as Latisse for eyelash growth and is used to get longer, fuller lashes, sometimes also on brows. Lash growth is well studied; reported iris colour change and periorbital fat loss are side effects of the drug family.

pyrilutamide.text: Pyrilutamide is a topical androgen receptor blocker being developed for pattern hair loss, and users see it as an alternative to oral DHT blockers. Trials so far have shown mixed results; it is not approved, and comparisons with RU58841 are mostly anecdotal.

ru58841.text: RU58841 is a topical antiandrogen bought from gray-market sellers by users hoping to treat hair loss without oral drug side effects. It was investigated for hair loss but never approved; human evidence is limited and the success reports come mainly from forum posts.

biotin.text: Biotin is a common supplement taken for hair and nail health, as well as beard and lash growth. It is essential to biology and deficiency affects hair, but benefits for people with normal intake are largely untested; high doses can interfere with some lab tests.

saw-palmetto.text: Saw palmetto is taken as a natural DHT blocker for male pattern hair loss, often as an alternative to finasteride. Small studies exist for hair, with weaker results than the approved drug; its main studied use is prostate symptoms.

pumpkin-seed-oil.text: Pumpkin seed oil is taken or applied in hopes of reversing male pattern hair loss. Small studies, including a multi-ingredient trial, reported more hair count; the effect of the oil alone is not isolated, and it is typically viewed as a minor option next to approved drugs.

collagen-peptides.text: Collagen peptides are taken for skin quality, wrinkles, hair, nails and joints. Several small trials report modest improvements in skin hydration and elasticity, many funded by supplement makers; effects on hair and on very high intake are less studied.

melatonin-topical.text: Topical melatonin is applied to the scalp by users hoping to slow hair loss, based on follicle receptors and antioxidant action. Small trials looked at hair-loss measures, but it is not an established treatment and most support comes from lab work and anecdote.

vitamin-d.text: Vitamin D is taken by users worried about hair loss, hormones, sleep and bone growth. Deficiency is linked to some hair conditions, but supplementation for hair or height in people with adequate levels is largely untested.

iron.text: Iron is supplemented by users with diffuse hair shedding or dark circles, who suspect low levels. Correcting a measured deficiency is studied for shedding; benefits for hair, beard or under-eyes with normal iron are untested.
